stops.name: Oxford, Beaumont Palace
stops.campa: On the eighth of September, in the King's own house at Beaumont outside the north gate of Oxford, Eleanor of Aquitaine bears her third son to Henry II of England. They name him Richard. He is not born to the English crown — two elder brothers stand before him, William already dead in infancy, Henry the Young King living — but he is born to Aquitaine, his mother's inheritance, and to the restless troubadour blood of her grandfather Duke William IX, first poet of the Provençal tongue. The bells of Oxford ring for a Plantagenet, not yet knowing which one.

stops.name: Poitiers, the court of Eleanor
stops.campa: Eleanor withdraws to Poitiers and gathers about her the poets of the Aquitainian tongue: Bernart de Ventadorn sings for her there, and the young Richard grows up inside the sound of the langue d'oc rather than the Anglo-Norman French of his father's court. He learns to make verses as other princes learn to hawk. In later years two of his own songs survive, a tenson traded with the Dauphin d'Alvernha and, from prison, a plainer song of his own grief — but the ear for it, and the grief it will one day carry, are shaped here, at his mother's knee.

stops.name: Poitiers and Limoges, the investiture as Duke of Aquitaine
stops.campa: At Poitiers, in the abbey church of Saint-Hilaire-le-Grand, the archbishop of Bordeaux and the bishop of Poitiers set the lance and banner of the duchy into Richard's hands: he is fourteen years old. Days later he enters Limoges in solemn procession and is given the ring of Saint Valerie, virgin martyr and patroness of Aquitaine, drawn from her own reliquary — mantle, coronet, sword, spurs, all laid on him in the old formula kept at Saint-Étienne. Aquitaine, which answers to no duke gladly, is told it now has one: Eleanor's son, crowned in his mother's country before he is crowned anywhere else.

stops.name: Taillebourg, the impregnable castle taken in three days
stops.campa: The barons of Poitou rise again, and Geoffroi de Rancon shuts himself inside Taillebourg, a rock fortress on the Charente held, the country says, by no power but God's — cliff on three sides, triple wall on the fourth. Richard does not storm it. He burns the fields and vineyards around it for a week, cuts off every road, until the garrison, starving, sallies out to break the siege and is routed in the open; Richard rides in through their own open gates on their heels. The impregnable castle falls in three days. No baron of the south doubts him again.

stops.name: Martel, the death of the Young King
stops.campa: Henry the Young King, crowned in his father's lifetime and never given power to match the crown, dies of a bloody flux at Martel in the Limousin, still in arms against both father and brother. On his deathbed he sends for a hairshirt and a rope, has himself laid on ashes with a stone for a pillow, and begs his father's forgiveness, which reaches him too late, by letter alone. Richard, his rival and heir in one, is now Henry II's eldest living son and undisputed heir to England, Normandy, Anjou, and his own Aquitaine besides — an inheritance bought with a brother's unquiet death.

stops.name: Tours, the taking of the cross
stops.campa: Word reaches Tours of the disaster at Hattin: Saladin has broken the army of Jerusalem, taken the True Cross, and by autumn the Holy City itself. Before his own father has so much as agreed to go, Richard — Count of Poitou, not yet king — kneels and takes the cross from the archbishop's hand, the first prince north of the Alps to do so. It is an act aimed as much at Henry II as at Saladin: the son moves before the father dares. He will spend two more years fighting Henry for the throne before he spends a single day fighting for Jerusalem.

stops.name: Chinon, the death of Henry II
stops.campa: Two days after his army breaks Henry's at Ballans, Richard learns his father is dying at Chinon. He rides to him and finds the old king already past speech, wasted by fever and by the discovery — the chroniclers say it broke him past the wound of any battle — that his youngest son John, his last hope, had also gone over to the rebels. Henry dies on the sixth of July. Richard kneels by the bier; the chroniclers report the corpse's nose bleeds afresh at his approach, an old ordeal-sign of a murderer's presence, and men whisper of it, though the Church absolves him.

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, the coronation
stops.campa: Richard is anointed and crowned in Westminster Abbey with the ancient rite: the oil on his breast, head, and hands, the mantle, the sword of justice, the crown set on him by the Archbishop of Canterbury. He has ordered that no Jew or woman cross the threshold of the feast that follows, a precaution too weak: that same evening a mob turns on the Jewish delegation come to bring gifts, and the massacre spreads by morning through the city and, in the weeks after, to York. Richard, furious, hangs some of the ringleaders — the crown he has just received is already stained with blood not his own.

stops.name: Vézelay, the meeting of the two kings
stops.campa: Beneath the great Romanesque tympanum of the Madeleine at Vézelay, where the Second Crusade was also preached, Richard and Philip Augustus of France meet with their combined armies and, on the fourth of July, set out together southward: two kings who trust each other only as far as the road requires, bound by oath not to attack each other's lands while the other is on crusade. Pilgrims and soldiers of a dozen tongues fill the hillside town. It is the largest army either king has commanded, and the last time the two of them will travel as allies rather than enemies.

stops.name: Marseille, awaiting the fleet
stops.campa: Richard reaches Marseille ahead of his own fleet, still beating down from England around Iberia, and will not wait: impatient by nature, he hires ships on the spot and sails on toward Sicily, working down the Italian coast — Genoa, Portofino, Pisa, Naples — visiting shrines and towns as a tourist-king might, while his official navy trails weeks behind him under its Dieppe captains. It is a pattern that will recur throughout the crusade: the plan made in council, and then Richard, unable to sit still inside it, moving faster than anyone expected him to move.

stops.name: Messina, the taking of the Griffon city
stops.campa: Messina, a Greek and Lombard town the crusaders call Griffon-land, quarrels with the newcomers over prices and lodging; Tancred of Lecce, the usurping King of Sicily, has also imprisoned Richard's widowed sister Joan, dowager queen, and withholds her dower. When a riot kills some of his men, Richard does not negotiate: at dawn on the fourth of October he storms the city, plants his standard on its walls before Philip's men have armed, and holds it as surety until Tancred releases Joan and pays a settlement in gold. Messina falls to a crusader king before a single blow is struck against the infidel.

stops.name: Messina, the abbot Joachim and the Antichrist
stops.campa: Wintering at Messina, Richard sends for Joachim of Fiore, the Calabrian abbot famous through Christendom for reading the Apocalypse of John as a map of ages still to come. Before the assembled court he asks the old man plainly when the Antichrist will be born and where. Joachim answers that he is born already, in the city of Rome, and will rise to the papal chair itself before the end. The court is troubled; Richard, setting out to fight one kind of enemy in the East, receives instead a prophecy pointed at the heart of Christendom, and rides on toward Jerusalem no less uneasy for it.
